procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 12.08.2020 passed by the High Court of Karnataka at Bengaluru in CRLP No.3164 of 2020, granting regular bail to Respondent No. 1.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court granted regular bail to Respondent No. 1 in CRLP No.3164 of 2020.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellant filed a Special Leave Petition which was converted to Criminal Appeal No. 3297 of 2023 challenging the High Court's order granting bail. The Supreme Court issued notice on 16.04.2021, and the matter was taken up for effective hearing on 27.03.2023. The Appellant was granted time to file an additional affidavit after complaints were received against Respondent No. 1 after his enlargement on regular bail. The Supreme Court ultimately allowed the appeal.

directions: the impugned order dated 12.08.2020 is set aside and the bail granted to Respondent No. 1 is hereby cancelled

issue.issue_text: Whether the bail granted to the accused should be cancelled in view of events subsequent to the grant of bail.

facts: The accused (Respondent No. 1), charged with conspiring to murder his wife, was granted bail.
After the bail was granted, the most crucial witnesses, who were the family members of the deceased, suddenly changed their stance.
The deceased's mother (the Appellant), who had initially named the accused as the main conspirator in her examination-in-chief, altered her testimony during cross-examination just 20 days later.
There were also past allegations against the accused of influencing police, hiring goons, and repeatedly assaulting the deceased.
law: While courts are generally reluctant to interfere with an order granting bail, it can be cancelled due to supervening circumstances that arise after the initial grant.
The concession of bail can be withdrawn if the accused misuses it by influencing witnesses, tampering with evidence, or otherwise attempting to evade the due course of justice.
Courts must balance the accused's right to liberty (Article 21) with the societal right to a fair and just trial.
application: The Court found that the "sudden change of stance" by the key witnesses so soon after the accused was released on bail was not a mere coincidence.
It established a "prima facie proximity" between the grant of bail and the accused having an "emboldening opportunity" to win over or influence the witnesses.
The Court connected this recent event with the accused's alleged past conduct (influencing police, hiring goons), concluding that he had the potential to interfere with the trial.
This influence over witnesses was considered a misuse of the concession of bail, which undermined the possibility of a fair and unbiased trial.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the accused had misused the liberty granted to him by influencing witnesses. To ensure a fair, just, and effective trial, the Court cancelled the bail granted to the accused.

issue.issue_text: Whether witnesses (PW-1, PW-4 and PW-5) should be recalled for further cross-examination for an effective, fair, and free adjudication of the trial.

facts: The key witnesses in the trial, PW-1, PW-4, and PW-5, are the mother, sister, and father of the deceased.
These witnesses turned hostile, with their testimony in cross-examination being 'diametrically opposite' to their examination-in-chief.
This change in their testimony occurred after the accused (Respondent No. 1) was granted bail.
Prior to this, the family members had been 'agitating vigorously' about the case since 2019.
The Court noted a 'prima facie proximity' between the grant of bail and the witnesses turning hostile, suggesting the accused had an opportunity to influence them.
law: The Supreme Court has vast powers under Article 142 of the Constitution and Section 311 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) to recall and re-examine witnesses.
This power can be exercised at any stage of a trial to meet the ends of justice and discover the truth.
The purpose of this power is not to fill gaps in the prosecution's case or prejudice the accused, but to gather evidence to 'scoop out the truth'.
application: The Court identified the family members (PW-1, PW-4, and PW-5) as the 'most crucial witnesses' to test the truth of the prosecution's allegations.
The fact that these witnesses completely resiled from their earlier vigorous stance was a compelling reason for the Court to intervene.
The Court determined that recalling these witnesses for further cross-examination was necessary for an 'effective, fair, and free adjudication of the trial'.
The Court invoked its powers under Article 142 and Section 311 CrPC to direct their recall, aiming to ensure they could testify in a congenial environment free from threat, fear, or inducement.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court found it to be a fit case to recall witnesses PW-1, PW-4, and PW-5 for further cross-examination. This decision was made to ensure a fair trial and to uncover the truth, given the witnesses' crucial role and their sudden, contradictory change in testimony after the accused was granted bail.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the bail granted to the accused should be cancelled in view of events subsequent to the grant of bail.
appellant_arguments: The High Court committed a grave error in overlooking the well-established principles for granting bail.
There is sufficient prima facie material indicating the respondent's involvement in a criminal conspiracy to kill his wife.
The respondent was misusing the concession of bail, as evidenced by complaints received against him after his release.
The respondent could influence vulnerable witnesses with his money and muscle power.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Where a court is satisfied that cogent and overwhelming circumstances indicate a misuse of the concession of bail, it is imperative for the court to withdraw such concession in the interest of justice.
obiter: Witnesses play a vital role in the administration of justice, and a witness turning hostile can cause irreversible damage to the credibility of the criminal justice system.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found a prima facie proximity between the grant of bail to the respondent and an emboldening opportunity for him to win over witnesses. Consequently, the court concluded that the respondent did not deserve to enjoy the concession of bail, at least until all crucial witnesses were examined, and that withdrawing this liberty was necessary to ensure an effective, fair, just, and unbiased conclusion of the trial.
legal_tests_applied: The test for cancelling bail is whether there are "cogent and overwhelming circumstances indicating misuse of concession of bail."
Courts must balance the individual's right to liberty under Article 21 with the right of an orderly society to a fair and unhampered trial.
Bail can be withdrawn if it is found that an undertrial has attempted to misuse the concession of bail by influencing witnesses, tampering with evidence, or trying to flee from justice.
why_respondent_won: The court was satisfied that there was a "prima facie proximity between the grant of bail to Respondent No.1 and an emboldening opportunity for him to win over the witnesses."

The court determined that the respondent did not deserve to enjoy the concession of bail until crucial witnesses were examined, as its withdrawal was necessary for an "effective, fair, just and unbiased conclusion of trial."
The court found it a fit case to recall witnesses (PW-1, PW-4 and PW-5) for further cross-examination in order "to reach an effective decision in the subject trial."
policy_considerations: Courts are under an onerous duty to ensure that the criminal justice system is vibrant and effective, that perpetrators do not go unpunished, and that witnesses are not under any threat or influence.

Witnesses play a vital role in the justice system, and if they turn hostile, it causes "irreversible damage to the administration of justice and the faith of the society at large in the efficacy and credibility of the criminal justice system will stand eroded and shattered."
The court must perform a "delicate balance" between the most precious right to liberty embodied in Article 21 and the right of an orderly society, which is committed to the rule of law.
